reviews: It was an outstanding experience, with extraordinary views of the three main pyramids from the rooftop where we enjoyed both dinner and breakfast. Meals were delicious! The rooms are excellent and freshly renovated. The three women who welcomed us and prepared our meals were incredibly warm and hospitable. Highly recommended!

This place has a long way to go before it can genuinely justify the glowing reviews it currently has. My family and I booked two rooms for two days based on the seemingly extraordinary feedback, but comparing it to reality, I can only assume most of those reviews are fake.

First, the location is far from ideal. While it’s not too far from the Pyramids’ main entrance, the hotel is tucked away on a back street that feels unsafe, especially at night. The area is crowded with camels and horses, and there are no facilities nearby, making it necessary to take a cab even for short trips. Walking feels risky, as scams or robberies could easily happen due to the isolated surroundings. Staying closer to the main entrance, where there are more people and a generally safer environment, is a much better choice.

Second, the rooms were awful, no matter what type you book. Queen, king – it makes no difference. The rooms reeked of smoke, the bed linens had holes from cigarette burns, and the ceilings were peeling and even falling in some places due to moisture. Almost all the furniture was broken, and the showers were poorly maintained. Some bathrooms didn’t have hot water, and the water pressure was inconsistent. To make matters worse, the Wi-Fi was unstable, and we couldn’t get a connection in the evening. Complaints to the owner were met with dismissiveness, as he told us to “be quiet” and refused to fix anything.

Third, the breakfast was another letdown. Despite being advertised as included, nothing was served on the first day. On the second day, we received a simple meal of eggs, cheese, beans, bread, and fries. However, during checkout, the owner demanded extra payment for the tea and coffee, claiming they weren’t part of the included breakfast – something no one mentioned when it was served.

This place is a complete sham. From the unsafe location to the poor condition of the facilities and the dishonest behavior of the owner, it was an extremely frustrating and disappointing experience. Unless you’re absolutely desperate, avoid this hotel. There are far better and safer options closer to the Pyramids’ main entrance.

reviews:
The lion statues of Qasr Nile in Cairo are bronze statues located at the ends of the Qasr El-Nil Bridge in Zamalek, Cairo, Egypt. They have become an iconic symbol of the city and a popular tourist attraction - so definitely a great place to stop and snap some pictures.
Every time you go to Zamalek and cross the bridge, you are welcomed by the bronze lions, posing with their heads held high and their manes flowing in the wind - I have had this opportunity a lot of times.

According to history, the lions were sculpted in France by a famous sculpture named Henri Alfred Jacquemart, and transported to Cairo. The lions of Qasr Nile serve as a reminder of Egypt’s rich history and cultural heritage. They also symbolize the city’s strength and resilience and are an important part of Cairo’s identity.
The lions on the Qasr al-Nil Bridge in Cairo are decorative and symbolic. They were installed in 1933 flanking the entrance to the bridge on either side, creating an iconic and grand gateway. … More

Visited 7 October 2022

Another free site to see in Cairo.

Walked to the most famous bridge over the River Nile in Cairo from Tahrir Square as it only a five minute walk.

Some great views of the city and the Nile can be seen from either end of the bridge as well as in the middle where you can really see how fast the current of the Nile is.
The most famous part of the bridge are the four large bronze lion sculptures which guard each end of the bridge.
It is very popular with locals and tourists alike.

This bridge, sometimes referred to as Kasr El Nil bridge was opened in 1933 by King Fouad and was originally called the Khedive Ismail Bridge in honour of his father. This was changed after the revolution that brought Nasser to power.

Interestingly the company that built this bridge was also constructing the Sydney Harbour Bridge at the same time.

reviews:
A comfortable, good-value stay in a quiet local neighbourhood, with reliable air conditioning, hot water and no hassles. Recommended for couples and independent travellers looking for something simpler and cheaper than big chains in Cairo.​

Overall stay
Stayed here as a couple and the place met exactly what we were looking for: a simple, clean base with working air conditioning and consistent hot water for showers. The price point is lower than the large international chains in Cairo, which makes it a good option if you want to control your budget without sacrificing basic comfort.​

Location and atmosphere
The property is in a local neighbourhood in the Dokki / Mohandessin area, so it feels more residential than touristy and gives a more authentic Cairo feel. Our unit faced the back street, which made it quiet enough for rest after sightseeing, and the area felt straightforward with no scams or tourist traps at the doorstep.​

Room and facilities
The apartment-style room comes with air conditioning, private bathroom with hot shower, and a small kitchen setup, which is handy if you like to prepare simple meals or drinks. The furnishings are modern and functional, and overall cleanliness and maintenance were in line with the rating and photos online.​

Who this suits
Would recommend Prime Select El Batal to couples and independent travellers planning to explore Cairo and Egypt who value a quiet, local base over a full-service hotel. If you are comfortable staying in an apartment-style property and do not need big-hotel facilities, this is a solid, good-value choice.​

I had a wonderful experience visiting this charming antique shop in the local bazaar. From the moment I stepped inside, I was captivated by the incredible variety of Egyptian cultural artifacts and traditional statues on display. Each piece tells a story — from beautifully crafted pharaonic figures to intricately detailed replicas of ancient gods and symbols.

The craftsmanship is exceptional, and you can truly feel the history and heritage reflected in every item. Whether you’re a collector, a history enthusiast, or simply looking for a unique souvenir to take home, this shop has something special for everyone.

The staff were friendly, knowledgeable, and happy to share insights about the origins and meanings of the pieces. I left with a stunning statue that now holds a place of pride in my home — it’s a perfect blend of artistry and cultural significance.

Highly recommend stopping by if you’re exploring the bazaar — this shop is a hidden gem that captures the spirit of Egypt beautifully! 🇪🇬

name: Italia Hotel Cairo
description: Italia Hotel Cairo, located at Address: 45 Champollion Street in the Downtown Cairo area of Cairo, is a much-loved hotel. reviews:
When we arrived, the building was completely locked. There was no bell, no instructions, and no response to calls or messages through the app. It was the middle of the night, the property is located in a deserted alley, and there was a parking area next to the building with around 20 stray dogs. We were alone, stuck outside, and felt genuinely unsafe.

Our taxi driver tried calling the landlord from a local phone multiple times. When he finally answered, the landlord said he would not let us in anymore and denied the early check in, contradicting his written messages. Only after the taxi driver mentioned calling the tourist police did someone finally open the door.

At reception, they then refused to give us the room, claiming it was not ready, and attempted to charge us 20 dollars for early check in because the tourist police had been mentioned. We had to insist strongly not to pay. While at reception, we noticed there are cameras clearly covering the entrance, meaning they could see us outside the entire time and still chose to ignore us.

We were forced to wait until 6.30 for the room to be “cleaned.” The cleaning was done in front of us with the door open and the protective sheet around the duvet was not changed. This is completely unsanitary.

The room itself had multiple serious issues. The air conditioning and heating did not work. Despite repeated messages through Booking.com, the landlord promised every day to bring a heater and never did. It was freezing cold. The bathroom door was broken, the toilet flush was broken and noisy all night, and the shower hose was damaged, spraying water in all directions, including onto the wall mounted hair dryer, creating a serious electrical hazard.

Breakfast was included in the booking, yet it was provided only once during the entire stay.

After we returned, the landlord falsely marked our booking as a no show, which I believe was done in anticipation of a refund request. Fortunately, I had kept photos of the property, a photo of the check in document we completed upon arrival, and full proof of my daily complaints through the Booking.com app chat. When Booking.com contacted me asking why we had not shown up, I provided all this evidence, and they resolved the issue appropriately, acknowledging what we went through.

This experience was unsafe, unhygienic, and handled with dishonesty and intimidation. I strongly advise others to avoid this property.

All the people working here were nice, naive, and helpful. They do not try to charge you extra for anything. Not like other places. The stay here is really cheap, plus the free breakfast with local food (been paste). We met amazing people, young staff members who try to earn a living with doing an honest job.

When you arrive in the neighborhood you may get confused about the small street with apartments. There are no signs of hotel at the street. It is a ramdom giza streer with local ladies and old men sitting outside etc. Mostşy there is a staff standing outside to guide you to the entrance. You will see a big apartment and when you walk to its entrance you will see the sign of the hotel.

You take the elevator to the 6th floor and on the right there is the reception. The rooms are in this floor. You may choose a room with a balcony or a large window, seeing the pyramids. Rooms clean, and have anything you would find in a hotel room e.g. kettle, tea bags etc.

On the upper floor there are 2 terrace, one is the cafe/restaurant with tables, and another one even a bit higher with no tables, and no lighting that you can see the view better. I spend hours and hours working in the cafe area. You may or may not order anything. Nobody asks/obliges you. There are a couple of food options, amd they have a dinner menu with soup, salad, rice and chicken. But I loved their biryani. Amazing rice and meat dish with spices.

The location is across the highway from the museum, and it may take a bit of time to walk there maybe 20 min etc, so we called an uber.

I will note, just to manage expectations, that I reserved their most basic room and it was quite compact. If you’re coming from the U.S. the size might surprise you. But it really was perfect. The bed was comfortable, the fridge was stocked with beverages that cost less than at the market, and the breakfast every morning was so so tasty. A fried egg, Egyptian pita with fig jam on the side, a couple kinds of cheese, fresh cucumbers and tomatoes, yogurt, coffee or tea. All of it every morning! Fatima also does a laundry service that is very affordable. It was less than $4 for a load (the charge is per item). It’s also important to note that if you’re used to US or tourist area hotels, this one may be hard to locate at first. It’s in a large building with businesses and (I think) residences. To get into the building you go through a hallway from the street. It’s lined with businesses with very friendly people. Then you take the elevator to Floor 2. On Floor 2 you’ll see the sign for the hotel. But you can stop anyone and ask for directions if you need to. I am a woman and was traveling alone; I felt very safe the whole time. Overall, I am so happy with my stay and will be at Olivia Hotel any time I’m in Cairo in the future!

description: Mausoleum of Shajar al-Durr, located at 20 El-Khalifa in the El Khalifa area of Cairo, is a go-to shrine. It is highly rated, holding a 4.4-star rating from 39 reviews and standing as a local spot. It remains a worthwhile stop for both locals and visitors to Cairo.

reviews: was destroyed by a bad restoration
Historical place

During the Seventh Crusade, when the Crusaders attacked Mansura in Egypt, her husband, the Ayyubid Sultan Salih Ayyub, died amidst the fierce fighting. Muazzam Turanshah, who had succeeded him, was assassinated, and on May 2, 1250, she was … More

Architecturally, the dome is distinctive in shape.

It has been restored in a way that has caused it to lose its original character.

This mausoleum was built in 1250 CE (648 AH) by Shajar al-Durr, wife of Sultan al-Salih Najm al-Din Ayyub, for her own burial place after her death. The mausoleum is square, with each side measuring approximately 7 meters internally. Each of the four sides of the mausoleum has a rectangular stucco niche, 205 cm wide, in the center. In the southeastern wing, there is a large mihrab surmounted by a semicircular arch.

The internal arches rest on a 46 cm wide wooden cornice, 283 cm above the floor of the mausoleum. This cornice surrounds the interior walls of the mausoleum and covers the door lintels. It also spans the niche of the mihrab and has been divided into 12 sections to encompass the curve of the niche. Inscriptions in Fatimid Kufic script are carved on the cornice. At a height of 5.40 meters from the floor of the mausoleum, there is another wooden cornice with an inscription in Naskh script, drawn in white.

From the moment I entered Madinaty, I felt like I had stepped into a different world a beautifully planned, peaceful, and green oasis right in the heart of Cairo. What truly sets Madinaty apart, though, is the sense of community. It’s a place where neighbors become friends, children play safely outdoors, and families can thrive in a wholesome, welcoming environment. Whether you’re raising a family, building a career, or enjoying retirement, Madinaty offers a balanced, joyful way of life.

I can’t recommend Madinaty enough. It’s more than a place to live it’s a place to belong. If you’re looking for a home that combines modern convenience with natural beauty, safety, and a warm community spirit, look no further. Madinaty isn’t just a neighborhood; it’s a lifestyle upgrade.

My stay at imperial pyramids view inn was an absolutely fantastic experience. This isn't a large, impersonal chain hotel; it's a charming, family-run guesthouse where the staff go above and beyond to make you feel welcome. The highlight, without a doubt, is the breathtaking, unobstructed view of the Giza Pyramids from the rooftop terrace. Enjoying breakfast and evening tea with that iconic view was unforgettable.

The rooms are clean, comfortable, and air-conditioned—a true blessing after a day in the Cairo heat. While the amenities are simple, you have everything you need, including reliable Wi-Fi. The location in the local neighborhood of Nazlet El-Semman feels authentic and is just a short walk from the Pyramids entrance.

What truly sets Amadeos apart is the hospitality. The owners are incredibly kind and helpful, offering great advice for tours and arranging a very reasonably priced airport transfer. If you're looking for a genuine, warm, and incredible-value stay right by the Pyramids, I cannot recommend imperial pyramids view inn enough.

Misleading and disappointing stay avoid this hotel
Unfortunately, we were deliberately misled by this hotel. On Booking.com, there are two different locations listed under the same name: Paradise Pyramids View Inn. One location has a swimming pool and better facilities, while the other does not. There is also a big price difference between the two.
Because of travel delays, we missed our scheduled taxi and were taken by another driver to the wrong location. Around 5:00 AM on July 19, the reception at the wrong hotel called the real Paradise Pyramids View Inn to ask for the correct address. To our surprise, the staff gave the address of their cheaper second location the one without a pool and with worse facilities.
We only found out the truth when we asked about the swimming pool around noon. Only then did they admit that we were staying at the wrong place.
Later, we were taken to the correct location, but there were no two rooms available. Instead, we got one room with three beds. This room was dirty, and both the room and the bathroom were in poor condition. The shower was full of mold and the floor was wet. I took photos as proof.
This felt like a clear case of intentional deception. Using the same hotel name for two different places on the platform is very confusing and unprofessional. I reported this to Booking.com before we left, and they said they would investigate but I haven’t heard anything back yet.
My advice: avoid this hotel. The chance of being misled and disappointed is just too high.

My partner and I throughly enjoyed our stay at the Four Pyramids Guest house and if we could rate it out of 10, we would give it a 12! If you want a true Egyptian experience, we highly recommend staying here. Mohamed was a hospitable, honest, reliable, and kind host, and we left the accommodation having made a good friend. He would stay with us on the lovely rooftop with a view of the Giza Pyramids in the evenings and we would chat for hours. The room was clean and tidy, and the hosts asked if we wanted it cleaned every day. If we needed anything at all, we would ask Mohamed and he would accommodate all our needs (whether that was bottles of water, or a driver to drive us around Egypt). We chose the breakfast included option, which was delicious every day (and served whenever we requested it to be the previous night). We should have paid for the dinner inclusive one when we booked, but instead we ended up paying per night (but this was so affordable and delicious, and it was very worth it) The dinner was 400 EGP per person, and there was so much food and variety of food we couldn’t even finish it all! All food was authentic and Egyptian, cooked by Mohamed’s mum - who is an excellent cook. We also booked tours with Mohamed, which included visiting tourist sites and riding a quad bike in the desert.

Unfortunately, on the last night my partner got ill and we had to push all our flights back. Mohamed and his family let us stay an extra night without any hesitation, took care of us, helped me get medicine for my partner, and took us to the doctors the next day. His mum made us a delicious warm soup - free of charge - to help him recover from the kindness of her heart. We can’t thank them enough. We will definitely stay here next time we visit Egypt.

reviews:
This place is a scam. I was in Egypt in August. I had emailed all my information to the building manager, however this person did not send me the correct address. I landed in Cairo with a child, called an uber and used the address in the profile. I was dropped infront of Madinaty Sports Club. It was 10pm. I started calling the number, after several calls, the guy texted. He would not give me the correct address until I would send him my passport picture again. So at 10:30, I sat with my child on the curb in busy traffic to take out my passport and send him the pictures again that I had previously emailed him and he had responded to that email. The manager had no remorse for his actions or empathy. He kept saying he doesn't read his emails. While I was stranded on the street with my child, he decided to tell me that the room did not have all the amenities that were described in the listing and if I would still proceed. The payment had already been made for this location. At 11:00pm, my phone was at 2% battery and I ask him to call an uber for me as I was not expecting this chaos. When my son and I finally got to the apartment, we had another shock. The place was filty, there was leftover food and drinks in the bedroom and the main area. The beds were not clean, the blankets had bad smell. I place looked rundown, nothing like the google and booking.com pictures. I took pictures and sent him again to get the beds changed as I could not put my child in that dirty bed. After another 30-40 minutes or so, the manager came and changed the bedsheet. On booking.com, the addressed used was of midanaty, however the location was a good 30-40 minutes from midanaty. My son was finally able to bed after midnight. The next day, we went out for breakfast, however the new address that was given to us was wrong as well. We were lost for 2 hours. Finally, I texted the guy again and then he called the uber for me. It was the stressful, unpleasant, and scary experience that we had on our first trip to Cairo. I was in Cairo for 10 days. We got out that place the next day. There is nothing Elite about this place.

A Hidden Gem in the Heart of the Nile!

We booked Gold Island Resort for a quick family escape and ended up completely hooked. The location alone is something special, an actual island in the middle of the Nile, just minutes from Cairo, yet it feels like a world away. Calm, quiet, and beautifully maintained.

The kids’ area kept them busy for hours, and the Nile Zoo on the island was a fun surprise small, but full of charm. Between that and the pool access, we genuinely had no reason to leave. The swimming pool was clean, peaceful, and perfect for a proper recharge.

reviews:
Staying at this hotel was one of the most terrible experiences I've ever had. Luckily, I only used it as a base and didn't stay there the whole time. Most of the time was spent sleeping and storing my luggage. The hotel is completely incapable of providing hotel service, even at a two-star level. There are reasons for this. The hotel doesn't clean the rooms. You have to ask several times. The cleaning staff are slow. They sit in the reception area smoking and chatting the whole time instead of doing their job. I stayed at this hotel for 23 days. The room was only cleaned about three times. Even then, only because I demanded it. The breakfast is extremely poor, and as the stay nears its end, breakfast items start to run out. The full breakfast consists of a boiled egg, bread warmed in a microwave (the worst way to warm bread, because it dehydrates and hardens it), a thin slice of cheese, a slice of ham the thickness of a hair, small processed items (honey, cheese, and guava paste, all very close to being fake), and coffee or tea, as you wish. The coffee is instant. There's almost never milk. The bread only arrives at 8:30 am, if it arrives at all. Once there was no bread, so the employee compensated me with another boiled egg. That was ridiculous. Note that the same employee who does the cleaning prepares the breakfast, which is absurd, as the functions should be separate. At the entrance, two men alternate as doormen. They do nothing and smoke all day. They watch the guests' lives all day and harass them with offers to make money. It was one of the worst things. Sometimes they offered haircuts, sometimes they asked for clothes, sometimes they asked for food if you arrived with those things. One of them even went so far as to ask me where I was going. When I told him what I was going to buy, he wanted to sell it to me. I recognize that this is part of the local culture, but these two men exaggerate. They do nothing and constantly bother the guests. The elevator looks extremely dangerous. There is no internal lining, so you can see the slab and the pillars. The hotel is very dirty. There is trash on the stairs and the elevator is filthy. The staff smoke all the time, except for those at reception. The reception is on the seventh floor, which requires an incredible effort to pick up and leave the key to leave. The street is extremely noisy. You hear everything as if it were all in the room. Cairo is very polluted, so opening the window there is dangerous, but sometimes it's necessary due to poor ventilation. The bathroom drain doesn't drain the water properly. You take a shower and the water level rises until it reaches your heels or higher. This only improved on the second-to-last day. Late at night, sometimes the shower water isn't hot. The hotel charges in dollars and resists giving you the change immediately, so it's best to give up and leave the change as a tip for someone who did nothing for you. The only advantages of this terrible place are its central location in Cairo, so you can easily get around by metro or Uber. Also, some of the staff are very kind and pleasant. They are not to blame. I believe the owner is to blame. He doesn't know how to manage accommodation.

I'll leave some tips here. There are two alternatives: be a conventional hotel or a self-catering establishment. In the first case, you need to fire the reception staff. They are useless because Cairo is very safe. There is no robbery, theft, or other violence. So they aren't watching anything. The person who does the cleaning can't be in charge of breakfast. Furthermore, you need someone to coordinate them because they clean whenever they want. They simply drag their feet. They don't use effective products. They just sweep and throw water around. A clean, fragrant, and disinfected room attracts guests. They need to learn how to clean. Breakfast could be set up on a table with two types of bread, one or two types of fruit, scrambled eggs, and juice. And an automatic coffee machine. Each guest serves themselves, and that's it. Stop this nonsense of trying to make an Egyptian breakfast, because it's not an Egyptian breakfast nowadays. I only ate falafel on the first day. Why so many people at reception? I counted about six people. One person working during the day and an alternating shift system at night would suffice. That reduces it to three or four employees. The boy who carries the luggage could be fired. He does nothing and smokes all day. Each guest can take their own luggage. There's no technology to manage the hotel. Everything is handwritten, which implies rework and wasted time. Install a computer with management software and start accepting credit cards. Remove those ridiculous holiday decorations. They're poorly made and look tacky, which gives the place a bad appearance. Currently, breakfast and other services are done on demand, which is absurd in a hotel. As a consequence, the hotel ends up buying things every day as needed, without stock. Therefore, it pays more. If it bought and stocked, it would be cheaper.Poucos funcionários dominam o inglês, exceto os da portaria, o que é um problema. Então capacite os funcionários para o mínimo. A pessoa que me serviu o café não sabia o que significava faca em inglês. In the second case, it's all very simple. Install automatic locks on the doors with a password that expires. Each guest can check themselves in. This eliminates all staff and breakfast. Cleaning can be outsourced to a company that provides full-service cleaning.

Sadly I have to agree with the majority of reviews that have been added here.
A friend made an arrangement for me to stay at this hotel, listed as a hostel, which it is not - no common rooms. After letting management know when I would arrive, my room wasn't ready. I was asked to wait for ten minutes. Ten minutes turned into one hour. The room I waited in was lovely, red balloons stuck to the ceiling, a jacuzzi in the corner, a well equipped bathroom, etc. The actual room I was given was the complete opposite. No beautiful bathroom, no jacuzzi (which was not a draw for me partly because Egypt is water starved and the consumption of water negative), no comfortable big bed. Instead I was given a room next to the office with three uncomfortable beds that included a door with no lock, hidden behind a moveable wardrobe, that accessed the office. I could hear everything that went on in the office 24x7. When I asked to change rooms I was told none were available.
The room itself featured a bathroom where the water intake to the toilet tank had to be turned off and on to prevent the room from flooding. I asked for a repair and what was provided made things even worse. The shower head fell off the first time I used the shower and was not replaced. The television was not connected to the satellite, the windows were difficult to open and the screens were full of fist sized holes. The doors to the balcony did not properly close allowing a rat to enter my room during the night. The bathroom doorjamb had protruding rusty nails, as did the frames on most of the beds. The sheets were pilly and the towels were old. The food that I ordered in was overpriced and underwhelming. In addition, the door to my room was difficult to lock and unlock. description: Mosque Taghri Bardi, located in the El Khalifa area of Cairo, is a standout mosque. It is exceptionally well rated, holding a 4.8-star rating from 29 reviews and standing as a local spot. It remains a worthwhile stop for both locals and visitors to Cairo.

reviews:
The Funerary Complex of Amir Taghribirdi or Mosque and Madrasa of Taghribirdi is a historical funerary complex of a mosque and madrasa built in the year 1440 during the Mamluk Sultanate.

This monument honors Amir Taghribirdi, the mosque's commissioner and the secretary to Sultan al-Zahir Jaqmaq. The mosque and madrasa of Taghribirdi is located on a corner of Saliba street.

The monument was founded in 1440 during the reign of Sultan al-Zahir Jaqmaq by Amir Taghribirdi. Amir Taghribirdi is not to be confused with his son, the famed Islamic scholar Ibn Taghribirdi.

Purportedly a man of somber disposition, Amir Taghribirdi rose to prominence as a respected amir under Sultan Barsbay for his role in leading the Mamluk army against the Crusader Kingdom of Cyprus.

For this achievement he was elevated to grand dawadar, or executive secretary, under Sultan al-Zahir Jaqmaq. However, Taghribirdi was murdered by his own mamluks shortly thereafter.

The mosque is facing negligence and not well maintained, i hope it will have more care from the authorities just like the rest of the beautiful historical mosques in the area.
I didn't visit it because it was closed when I passed by on my way to the Mosque of Ahmad Ibn Tulun. But as is usual with Islamic mosques, it stands tall and beautiful.

The Tughri Bardi Mosque is one of the lesser-known mosques, but it's a hidden architectural gem on Saliba Street in Cairo. It tells the story of an important Mamluk prince who lived during a transitional period following the Bahri Mamluk … More

An ancient historical mosque

Prince Taghribirdi built his mosque in 844 AH (1440 CE) on an area of ​​80 square meters. It has a large, square entrance with a wooden door to the right leading to the qibla (direction of prayer). The mosque was built according to the orthogonal plan of madrasas (religious schools), consisting of an open courtyard that was originally roofed. The courtyard is bordered by two large iwans (vaulted halls) on the eastern and western sides, and two smaller ones on the northern and southern sides. All of these iwans are open with arches topped by decorative panels inscribed with Quranic verses. These iwans are roofed and decorated with various colors.

The mosque is divided into three sections: the iwan, the women's prayer area, and the kuttab (Quranic school). There is also a large courtyard beneath the mosque containing two underground passages that run the length of the mosque. Locals and visitors alike claim that Prince Taghribirdi used these passages as a prison to punish those who disobeyed his orders, but there is no evidence to support this claim.

The Taghri Bardi Mosque is 594 years old, but its condition is no different from that of many of our forgotten and neglected monuments.

Despite its long history, the mosque has faded from the memory of officials and has found no one to care for or maintain it, neither from the Ministry of Religious Endowments nor the Ministry of Antiquities.

It was built in 844 AH (1440 CE) by Prince Ibn Taghri Bardi, who was Yusuf ibn Taghri Bardi ibn Abdullah Jamal al-Din Abu al-Mahasin ibn Prince Sayf al-Din al-Zahiri, Atabeg of the Army in Egypt. … More

One of the important public fountains in Cairo is the Sabil, built in 1479 AD. You can easily reach it on foot from Citadel Square, as it's very close, and also near the Khalifa fire station. It's a freestanding building from its inception, … More

Historical Overview and Definition
Full Name: Sultan Qaytbay's Sabil and Kuttab
Built in 884 AH / 1479 AD by order of the Mamluk Sultan Al-Ashraf Qaytbay.
Located at the beginning of Al-Saliba Street off the Citadel Square, adjacent to Shaykhun Street, in the Khalifa district of Cairo.
Function and Architectural Structure
Purpose of the Building:
• A fountain for distributing drinking water to passersby throughout the ages.
• A Kuttab (school) on the upper floors, to teach children the basics of reading, writing, and Quranic memorization.
The general structure consists of several levels:
• The first underground level: A hidden water cistern filled with water to feed the qirura or fountain openings.
• The second level above ground: The room from which water was served to passersby through windows or grated openings.
• The third level: The Kuttab—the educational level—where lessons were held for children.
The building has two prominent facades: the main facade overlooks Al-Saliba/Shaykhun Street, and a second side facade. Entrance: High, narrow, decorated with a trilobite arch and colored stone and marble motifs.
Decoration: A combination of floral and geometric motifs and epigraphic inscriptions, engraved on stone and marble.
Foundation Text: There is a large foundation plaque made of colored marble/stone, divided into nine sections spread over three levels, containing ministerial inscriptions and inscriptions establishing the sabil's construction.
Features and Distinctions
It is considered the first independent sabil in Egypt to be built independently, rather than attached to a mosque, school, or house—that is, it stood alone as an independent charitable structure.
The architecture is considered the pinnacle of Mamluk-era decoration and artistic precision.
It includes the names of Sultan Qaitbay in capitals and commemorative inscriptions as a kind of architectural signature.
The design of the entrance and some of the decorations resemble those of the entrance at the Al-Ashrafiya School in Jerusalem in terms of artistic composition.
Location and Access
You can reach it via Al-Saliba Street to Sheikhoun Street.
The fountain is located near the end of Al-Saliba Street, towards Salah El-Din Square/Citadel, on the right of those heading towards the Citadel.

The cleaning lady’s attitude was unbelievably rude, acting as if I had no right to be upset and as if she was entitled to enter whenever she wanted because she “wanted to finish early.” That is not hospitality; that is disrespect.
This hostel is dirty, chaotic, noisy, poorly maintained, and run by an entirely unqualified team who have no understanding of hospitality whatsoever.

One star is far too generous. I will never return, and I strongly warn others to stay away from this place

SCAM! Don’t go to this hotel!

It was a miserable experience. We went with my family (4 of us) for 3 nights. We booked the “ Quadruple Room with Balcony - Pyramids View” and got something completely different.
The pictures on booking of the room we booked look like a very clean and modern/new room, with a view from the hole bedroom to the three pyramids. Instead we received a dirty room, with used sheet beds and towels that smelled super bad. The toilet with humidity and rust everywhere, un functioning and dirty toilet. NO view of the three pyramids.

We had to pay in cash in advance before even seeing the room. Once we saw the room we immediately went to say this was not the room we asked and payed for (the balcony room was indeed much more expensive than the others). Then they told us that booking had a problem, and the room we originally booked and payed for was full. They said the day after they would solved this.

Two days passed, and every time we would ask about this the smily girl of the reception would told us she was trying to solve this with the manager and she would let us know. Of course, the last day we realized this was just excuses and they would never refund us.

So we went there to the reception and asked them gently again. we wanted a refund of the difference of the price from the room we booked and the one we stayed (in booking it was 130€ difference for the three nights we stayed). We asked them this in a very nice way but we were determined. They said it was not their fault but booking, and the only thing they could do was offer us a dinner.

We were very determined and after one hour and a half of insisting what was fair, they refund us.

Still, horrible experience, and we could see they would do this with other people and rooms. They even change the name of the hotel so that bad reviews confuse the costumers.

I was in Cairo from August 2nd -1tth, 2025. Initially I had booked a different apartment/hotel which turn out to be a scam. At 12am midnight, i was looking for a new place for myself. The location and apartment were very clean. We were looking for something near Madinaty Squash Club, it was 5 minutes drive, exactly what we wanted. Going through an awful first night, we were thankful that we were in a safe place. Our 8 day stay at this location was extremely comfortable. My son said "whenever we come to Cario, this is where we will stay, it feels home." The owner was very responsive and helpful. The doors had automatic locks which made it pretty safe. The air conditioning in all rooms worked great. The bathroom was very clean. If anyone is looking into an Air B&B, I will strongly recommend this place. Thank you for helping us in the awful situation that my son and I were in on Aug 2nd.

Prepare to be kicked out of the apartment at checkout!!!

When booking on Booking.com, I requested a late checkout because my flight departs at 11:50 PM. They told me "there was no problem."

On the day of my arrival, they started telling me the checkout was at noon at the latest. I showed them the conversation, and they said there was no problem, but I had a bad feeling about it.

Sure enough, on the day of arrival, I was kicked out of the apartment at 12:15 PM!!!

So I went to the lobby because I had no other option, and there I was, kicked out of the lobby!!!!

In the lobby, the hostess walked right past me, looking down her nose at me, and then came back to ask what I was doing there. I explained the situation (she didn't understand anything; she asked me several times for the room number in English, and I answered in English, but apparently it didn't register). Then she told me, "It's not possible; this isn't a hotel. You have to leave the lobby."

Unacceptable! If I had known beforehand, I would have booked an extra night or stayed somewhere else.

So I spent 11 hours waiting at the airport (it was difficult to do anything else with my suitcases, which couldn't be stored there either).

The moral of the story is: once you've paid, get out quickly.

Otherwise, the apartment was clean, but it overlooked a landfill. When we arrived by taxi, we were also refused entry, even though we showed our reservation.

🕌 Mosque of Sultan Qaitbay 🕌

#Manial
#Cairo Governorate

🕌 The Qaitbay Mosque in Manial al-Rawda is an ancient mosque over 600 years old. It was built by Sultan Al-Ashraf Abu Al-Nasr Qaitbay and its construction was completed in 1491 AD, after ten years of work. 📿

🕌 The site of the mosque was originally occupied by another mosque built during the reign of Al-Nasir Qalawun. However, prayers ceased there after it was damaged and fell into disrepair. 📿

🕌 Sultan Qaitbay ordered its demolition and built his current mosque in its place. He expanded its area and added gardens and buildings around it. 📿

🕌 However, in 1801 AD, the mosque burned down due to the explosion of a gunpowder store located next to it. The fire consumed most of its old wooden elements. Therefore, this mosque is considered the least ornate of the mosques built by Qaitbay. The last restoration of the mosque was in 2004. 📿

The **Warraqiya Dudu Sabil** is one of the most magnificent Ottoman sabils in Cairo, located on Souq al-Silah Street in the Darb al-Ahmar district. This sabil is distinguished by its unique architectural beauty and the poignant story of its construction.

### **The Story of the Founder and the Name**

* **The Founder:** It was built by Mrs. **Badawiya Shahin** in **1761 CE (1174 AH)**.

* **The Reason for the Name:** Mrs. Badawiya established it as a perpetual charity in memory of her young daughter, **Ruqayya Dudu** (the word "Dudu" was an Ottoman title used for ladies and girls as a term of endearment and respect). Ruqayya was the daughter of Prince **Ridwan Kashif al-Jalfi**, one of the prominent Mamluk princes of that era.

---

### **Architectural Creativity (Ottoman Rococo Style)**

This public fountain is considered a masterpiece because it was built during a period when Ottoman architecture was influenced by the European Rococo style, as evidenced by the delicate curves and floral decorations:

* **The Arched Facade:** Unlike older fountains with flat facades, the Ruqayya Dudu fountain features an arched (semi-circular) copper facade with three windows for dispensing water, adorned with exquisitely crafted copper grilles.

* **Decorations:** The stone facade is richly decorated with carved floral motifs, and above the windows are commemorative plaques inscribed in elegant Arabic calligraphy, containing Quranic verses and lines of poetry praising water and bounty.

* **The Quranic School:** Above the fountain is a second story that served as a Quranic school for the neighborhood children. It features beautiful wooden mashrabiyas overlooking Souq al-Silah Street.

---

### **Location and Significance**

* **Address:** Souq al-Silah Street, Al-Darb al-Ahmar, Cairo.

* **Neighbors:** The sabil is located in a rich historical area, adjacent to the **Al-Jay al-Yusufi Mosque** and the **Bab Manjak al-Silahdar**, making it an essential stop on any tour of Fatimid and Mamluk Cairo.

---

### **Visiting Information**

* **Opening Times:** The monument is usually open to visitors from **9:00 AM to 5:00 PM**.

* **Experience:** Standing before this sabil, you will appreciate the refined artistic taste of the 18th century and how grief over the loss of a daughter was transformed into a charitable and architectural work that has endured for centuries, quenching the thirst of passersby and educating children.

reviews: The Citadel of Cairo or Citadel of Salah ad-Din(‎ Qalaʿat Salāḥ ad-Dīn) is a medieval Islamic-era fortification in Cairo, Egypt, built by Salah ad-Din (Saladin) and further developed by subsequent Egyptian rulers. It was the seat of government in Egypt and the residence of its rulers for nearly 700 years from the 13th to the 19th centuries. Its location on a promontory of the Mokattam hills near the center of Cairo commands a strategic position overlooking the city and dominating its skyline. At the time of its construction, it was among the most impressive and ambitious military fortification projects of its time.[2] It is now a preserved historic site, including mosques and museums
Amazing place
🏰 Citadel of the Mountain (Saladin's Citadel) – Mother of Cairo’s Historic Citadels … More

The main entrance to the Citadel of the Mountain, known as "Saladin's," leads visitors past the Al-Gawhara Palace (the former residence of Muhammad Ali Pasha), then to the Qalawun Mosque and the Muhammad Ali Mosque, before proceeding to the Police Museum and the Citadel Prison. It overlooks Salah Salem Street. A notable feature of the Citadel during Ramadan is the Iftar cannon, which fires daily at sunset to announce the end of the day's fast and the start of Iftar. This beautiful, inherited tradition is unique to Egypt, the cradle of civilization.

One of the most enjoyable places in Cairo is the Citadel of Saladin, which contains the Mosque of Muhammad Ali, the Mosque of Al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, the Military Museum, and the Police Museum. Opening hours are from 8:00 AM to 4:00 … More

Sultan Qaitbay’s Wakala is a historic building in Cairo that exemplifies Mamluk-era architecture and urban planning. A wakala (or caravanserai) traditionally served as a commercial and residential complex for merchants, combining shops, storage spaces, and accommodations in one elegant structure.

The building features finely crafted stonework, intricate inscriptions, and beautiful arches that highlight the sophistication of Mamluk design. Visitors can admire the harmonious proportions and decorative details, reflecting the artistic and functional ingenuity of the period.

Located in historic Cairo, Sultan Qaitbay’s Wakala offers insight into the commercial, social, and architectural life of the city during the Mamluk era. It’s a fascinating site for history enthusiasts, architecture lovers, and anyone interested in exploring Cairo’s rich cultural heritage.

Alfred Chammas Palace is one of the oldest palaces in Heliopolis. Its owner was a merchant of Levantine origins who lived in Egypt and built this palace there. He placed two initials of his name in English on its gate. The palace is located next to the Evangelical Church and overlooks Al-Thawra Street on one side and Cleopatra Street on the other. King Farouk gifted it to his bride, Safinaz Zulfikar (Queen Farida), so she could stay there while preparing for their wedding. The palace then returned to its owner and was later sold to several owners, including the former ruler of Sharjah, Sheikh Saqr. One of the most important landmarks in the Heliopolis district and one of its … More

#Alfred_Shamas_Palace
One of the most important and oldest palaces in Heliopolis, it is located next to the Evangelical Church and overlooks Al-Thawra Street on one side and Cleopatra Street on the other.

The owner of the palace is: Alfred Shamas
He was a merchant of Levantine origin who lived in Egypt. The first three letters of his name in English are inscribed on the main gate of the palace.

The style used is #Neo-Gothic, a decorative and stylized style that emphasizes the structural expressions and strength of the building through towers and arches, within a framework of exaggerated ornamentation. Exposed brick and smooth whitewash create a visual contrast and harmony, along with the use of supporting arches and corbels.

The palace's importance stems not only from its distinctive architectural style but also from its role as the site of one of the most important royal weddings. King Farouk rented it to Safinaz Zulfikar, #Queen_Farida, to reside in after her family moved from Alexandria to Cairo to prepare for the wedding. #King_Farouk visited her there regularly. On January 19, 1938, the palace facades were adorned with lights and colorful banners in preparation for the wedding. The people of Heliopolis gathered in front of the palace to see the bride. Musical groups performed on the wedding night, Arabian horses presented their dances, and the owners of neighboring palaces decorated theirs. Queen Farida then proceeded from the Farid Shamas Palace to the Qubba Palace, becoming queen on her wedding day, January 20, 1938.

I am surprised that I haven't been able to find out who designed this magnificent palace. None of the books I have consulted mention its designer, and I haven't found any information about it online!

reviews: Here, History talks !

Lajin Al-Sayfi Mosque This mosque was built by Prince Lajin Hussam Al-Din Al-Jerkasi, who was brought by Al-Khawaja Kazil as a young child. Then King Al-Zahir Barquq bought him (Ibn Iyas: p. 24). Hence, his name Al-Zahir was added to his … More

The mosque is an ancient monument and it is not appropriate for the Ministry of Antiquities and Endowments to neglect its restoration in this manner. The restoration must be completed quickly so that worshippers can pray. The mosque was built in 1449 AD during the Mamluk era.

The mosque was built by Prince Lajin Husam al-Din, a Circassian, who was brought to the sultanate as a young child by Khawaja Kazil. Sultan al-Zahir Barquq purchased him, and he was subsequently given the title al-Zahiri and became one of his Mamluks. After several transfers and changes of ownership, he was eventually purchased by his master, Sultan al-Zahir Jaqmaq, also a Circassian, before the latter ascended the sultanate. This occurred before 836 AH (1438/1439 CE), and he was then freed. Lajin became known as Lajin al-Zahiri Jaqmaq.

The Mosque of Prince Lajin al-Sayfi is relatively small, measuring approximately 25 meters in length and 21 meters in width. It consists of an open courtyard in the center, measuring 6 x 9 meters, with the flooring lower in the surrounding arcades. The courtyard is surrounded by arcades on all sides.

It was built by the Circassian Mamluk prince Husam al-Din Lajin al-Zahiri Jaqmaq in 853 AH/1449 CE. Located on Abdul Majid al-Labban Street (formerly Marasina Street) in the Sayyida Zeinab district of Cairo, this mosque is one of the few … More

The Khanqah of Baybars al-Jashankir: The Story of a Sultan and a Tragic End in the Heart of al-Gamaliya

The Khanqah of Sultan al-Muzaffar Baybars al-Jashankir stands in the historic al-Gamaliya district as one of the oldest and most important surviving khanqahs (Sufi lodges) in Cairo. This majestic architectural monument not only tells the story of the evolution of Mamluk architecture but also the dramatic tale of a prince who rose to the pinnacle of power only to meet a tragic end at the hands of the sultan who overthrew him.

Who was Baybars al-Jashankir?

Baybars al-Jashankir was not the famous Mamluk sultan al-Zahir Baybars al-Bunduqdari, but rather another prince who succeeded him.

Origin and Position: He was of Circassian origin and a Mamluk of Sultan al-Mansur Qalawun. He rose through the ranks until he reached the prestigious position of "al-Jashankir," whose holder was responsible for tasting the sultan's food and drink to ensure it was free of poison.

Rise to Power: During the second reign of the young Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, Baybars al-Jashankir and Prince Salar were the de facto rulers of the country. When al-Nasir Muhammad decided to abdicate and go to Karak, the two princes seized the opportunity, and Baybars al-Jashankir was installed as Sultan of Egypt in 1308 CE, taking the title al-Malik al-Muzaffar Rukn al-Din Baybars.

The Tragic End: His reign was short-lived. Less than a year later, Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad returned to Cairo with force and reclaimed his throne. Baybars al-Jashankir was arrested and executed by strangulation on al-Nasir Muhammad's orders in 1309 CE. He was not buried in the magnificent dome he had prepared for himself in this khanqah (Sufi lodge).

A Unique Architectural Masterpiece: Baybars al-Jashankir began building this massive khanqah in 1306 CE while still a prince and completed it in 1309 CE as Sultan. It is the oldest khanqah still standing in Cairo.

Location: Situated on Al-Gamaliya Street, it was built on part of the grounds of the Great Fatimid Ministry.

Function: It served as a comprehensive complex to house approximately 400 Sufis, providing them with food, drink, and lodging. It also functioned as a center for teaching Hadith (Prophetic traditions) and reciting the Quran.

Architectural Description:

Main Entrance: One of the most magnificent Mamluk entrances, it is a soaring gateway clad in colored marble, surmounted by a three-lobed arch (Madaini), and adorned with Quranic inscriptions and carvings.

Mausoleum Dome: The dome is one of the oldest large stone domes in Mamluk architecture, distinguished by its simplicity and grandeur. Although it was intended as the burial place for Baybars, he was not buried there.

Minaret: The most unique element of the building, it stands out from all other minarets in Cairo. Its spire (kasq) is not octagonal as is typical, but rather a square, cylindrical structure topped by a small, ribbed dome. This design is unique and has not been replicated in any other minaret.

Interior Design: It consists of a central courtyard surrounded by four iwans, the largest being the qibla iwan, in addition to Sufi cells (khalwas) distributed over several floors.

Current Status (July 2025): The Khanqah of Baybars al-Jashankir is a registered Islamic monument open to visitors. It has undergone restoration at various times to preserve it. Although not as famous as the mosques of the great sultans, it remains a key destination for those interested in Islamic architecture, especially to admire its magnificent entrance and its unique, unparalleled minaret.

A visit to the khanqah is a journey into the heart of the Mamluk era, where the stones tell the story of a powerful prince's ambition, the ingenuity of creative architects, and the dramatic end of a sultan who found no peace in his reign or even in his grave.

One of Cairo's most important historical monuments – the equestrian statue of Ibrahim Pasha, son of Muhammad Ali and a prominent 19th-century military commander. Created in 1872 by the French sculptor Charles Cordier at the request of Khedive Ismail, who wished to honor his father's memory. Originally located in Ataba Square, it was later moved to Opera Square. It has a controversial history: Cordier also created two bas-reliefs commemorating Egyptian victories over the Turks – Istanbul protested, and the plaques were never installed (they ended up in France). The monument has survived turbulent times, criticized by Urabi's supporters as a symbol of Muhammad Ali's dynasty. It underwent renovation in 2016. The bronze horseman on a marble pedestal dominates the square. Access is free, 24 hours a day. Metro: Opera station.

Tucked away in the lavish Al Manial Palace, the mosque here is a stunning little surprise. Its less famous than Cairo's grand mosques, but feels 'cosier', and is dripping with charm and intricate detail.

The whole palace complex is extravagent, and the mosque feels quieter, more contemplative, but is still filled with stunning tilework and a fantastic carved ceiling.

Magnificent architecture

The mosque is part of the Prince Muhammad Ali Palace complex. The mosque and minaret are of a different style, but both are masterpieces in their form, design, and beautiful carvings. The mosque is open for visits, not for prayer. For … More

The Muhammad Ali Palace Mosque, distinguished from the outside by its diverse decorative elements and exquisite inscriptions executed in Arabic calligraphy in the Islamic style, has two plaques on either side of the entrance. The right plaque contains the mosque's founding text, while the other lists the names of the workers and artists involved in its construction, as well as the date of its founding, 1352 AH. The plaques read: "This blessed mosque was built by Prince Muhammad Ali, son of the late Khedive Muhammad Tawfiq Pasha, may God have mercy on him. The calligraphy is by Hajj Ahmad Kamal Effendi, head calligrapher in Istanbul. The carpentry, drawings, and copper work are by Master Muhammad Ibrahim al-Najjar. The carpets are by Master Muhammad Ibrahim Talha. The marble is by Masters Ahmad Sukkar and Mahmoud Saleh. The stonework is by Master Muhammad Afifi al-Najjar. The tiles are made in Istanbul. The construction was by Master Ahmad Mahmoud al-Banna and his sons. These works were overseen by Suleiman Effendi Metwally Pasha, the clerk of the department, and were completed in the year 1352 AH." The mosque is decorated on the outside with sandstone, while the walls are decorated in the form of carpets of different styles. The windows are in the form of arches surrounded by bands of geometric decorations, and the courtyard of each window is designed with marble decorated in the form of Mamluk-style star-shaped plates made in Italy. From the eastern wall protrudes the mihrab block in the form of a pointed arch, below which is a square of Kashani tiles. The mosque is distinguished by the presence of a dome surmounted by a band with Qur’anic writing in the foliated Kufic script and many decorative bands of plants and geometrics. The mosque is a rectangular space divided internally into two sections. The eastern section contains the minbar and the mihrab, while the western section includes the reciter’s chair made of wood and decorated with gilded Qur’anic verses. The walls of the mosque are covered with magnificent ceramic tiles, and its wooden ceiling is decorated with gilded decorations.

Sultan Mahmud's Sabil (public fountain) in Sikkat al-Habaniyah, Port Said Street

This sabil, along with the madrasa (religious school), was built by Sultan Mahmud Khan, son of Sultan Mustafa Khan, who assumed power after the deposition of Sultan Ahmed in 1164 AH/1750 CE. The foundation inscription on the door of the sabil-madrasa indicates that the actual founder of the architectural complex was Prince Bashir Agha, the agent of Dar al-Sa'ada (the royal court), and it bears the name of Sultan Mahmud Khan, son of Mustafa Khan.

It is known for its architectural function as both a Sufi lodge and a school. Originally, it was a school established by Sultan Mahmud Khan so that he would pass by its gate. It included living quarters for Sufis and a well-stocked library. A public water fountain was added next to it for the general public and passersby to drink from. Above the fountain was a school for teaching children writing and the Quran. Over time, the school was transformed into a Sufi lodge for dervishes and Sufis.

The school's courtyard is surrounded on all four sides by a portico supported by a single row of columns that bear arches overlooking the courtyard. Behind each of these porticoes are small rooms known as "khalawi," which were used by students when it was used as a school. Later, after its transformation into a Sufi lodge, they became dormitories for dervishes and Sufis.

The southern portico, however, does not contain any khalawi. It is occupied by a study or teaching area that also served as a mosque, as evidenced by the mihrab (prayer niche) that still exists there.

🕌 Sultan Mahmud Khan Tekke, Sabil, and Kuttab – One of the Most Magnificent Ottoman Buildings in Cairo
The Sultan Mahmud Khan Tekke is the first and largest tekke actually established … More

A magnificent Ottoman work... Located on Habbaniye Street, this small complex, consisting of a madrasa and a fountain (sebilküttâb), was built in 1751 by Moralı Beşir Ağa, the Agha of the Darüssaâde (Dârüssaâde) in the name of Mahmud I, according to its inscriptions. The madrasa currently serves as the Southern Inspection Building of the Egyptian Antiquities Authority. The fountain (sebilküttâb), which was renovated in 1883 and 1952, has undergone several recent renovations.

The portal is located in the center of the northwest facade facing Port Said Street. The madrasa, which stretches 41.5 meters from the fountain (sebilküttâb) at the west corner, has a two-story façade. The ground floor houses a total of ten shops, four to the right of the portal and six to the left. These shops, now slightly below road level, are covered with barrel vaults. On the upper floor, a total of eight rectangular windows with iron bars are located, three to the right and five to the left of the portal. Above and below these are two decorative bands of vegetal motifs running the entire façade.

The Sultan Mahmud Madrasa, a Cairo madrasa from the Ottoman period, parallels the Ayyubid and Mamluk madrasas in terms of teaching Sunni Islam. Its layout and spatial concept are more closely similar to educational institutions in Anatolia. Its courtyard plan, surrounded on four sides by porticoes and cells, resembles the madrasas of Bayezid II in Edirne (1488), Kılıç Ali Pasha in Tophane (1580), and Sultan Ahmed (1609-1616), Damad Ibrahim Pasha in Nevşehir (1726-1727), and Nuruosmaniye in Istanbul (1755). On the other hand, although the adjacent sebilküttâb appears to be a Mamluk building type, its semicircular projection resembles the public fountains in the capital. In fact, this structure is the first semicircular sebilküttâb in Cairo. Therefore, it is understood to have pioneered later structures.

The Sultan Mahmud Madrasa and Sebilküttâb, a striking example of how Ottoman civilization and culture were transmitted to the provinces, still stands and holds a significant place in Cairo's architectural heritage, a site visited by many locals and foreigners.

reviews: Perfect experience

Egypt Bazaar, owned by Mohamed Reda Ali, is a place that blends refined taste with authentic Egyptian charm in the heart of Cairo. The shop specializes in ceramics, mother-of-pearl items, chairs, gift boxes, and jewelry cabinets, all crafted with meticulous attention to detail and beauty. Each piece reflects a unique artistic touch, showcasing Egypt's rich heritage of handicrafts. The staff are exceptionally courteous and respectful, greeting visitors with genuine smiles and warm Egyptian hospitality, making the experience even more enjoyable.

Located in the heart of Cairo, Egypt Bazaar feels like a piece of history brought to life amidst the hustle and bustle of the modern city. From the moment you step inside, you feel transported to another world, filled with colors, aromas, and sounds that tell the story of both ancient and modern Egypt. The narrow passageways, brimming with handcrafted goods, embroidered fabrics, and copper lamps casting their golden light on the stone walls, create a magical atmosphere that captivates the senses and offers an unforgettable experience. Vendors stroll about with genuine Egyptian smiles, displaying their wares with skill and enthusiasm, explaining the story behind each piece as if it were a work of art imbued with the spirit of its creator. A medley of voices—the vendors' calls, the laughter of shoppers, and the lively haggling—adds a special charm to the shopping experience. The aroma of spices fills the air, mingling with the scents of leather, oriental perfumes, and incense, creating a journey through time that blends authenticity with refined taste.

The bazaar boasts a wide array of souvenirs, from expertly crafted replicas of Pharaonic jewelry to luxurious cotton fabrics and copper and silver artifacts. There are also small corners showcasing traditional arts such as papyrus painting, pottery, and wood carving, each corner telling a different facet of Egypt's rich heritage.

What distinguishes Egypt Bazaar is that it offers more than just products; it provides a complete experience. The vendors are warm and welcoming, and the bazaar itself is tastefully organized and decorated, blending a touristy aesthetic with an authentic, local atmosphere. Even sitting in the small café at the end of the tour, enjoying Egyptian coffee and mint tea, gives you a sense of comfort and makes you feel like you're part of this beautiful world.

At the end of the visit, the visitor leaves laden not only with purchases, but also with memories, photos, and experiences that embody the beauty and true spirit of Egypt. Egypt Bazaar is more than just a market; it's a journey into the heart of Egyptian culture and a window into a long history of creativity, craftsmanship, and the generosity that has characterized Egyptians throughout the ages.

If you're looking for the best Egyptian handicrafts and souvenirs, plus friendliness, hospitality, and good friends, this is the perfect place. We were so happy to spend two afternoons having tea with new friends.

reviews:
One of the main historical Sabeels of Cairo that dates back to Ottoman times.

Founded in 1630, the foundation inscription of this sabil indicates that its construction was commissioned jointly by Prince Mustafa Jalabi Sinan Pasha-Zade and Muhammad Agha.

This sabil is an independent structure, and it originally had a kuttab (Qur’anic school) on top, which has since disappeared.

The building consists of two façades: One faces Al-Ja’i Al-Yousifi Mosque and is decorated with ceramic tile panels featuring distinctive ornamental designs, and the other faces Souq Al-Silah Street and contains the main functional openings.

A distinctive architectural feature of this sabil is that it is considered the first Ottoman-era sabil in Cairo to include an attached prayer space (mushalla) within its structure, reflecting a unique design that combines both charitable/public service functions and religious worship within a single architectural unit.

description: Mastabat Al-Mahmal, located in the El Khalifa area of Cairo, is a standout landmark. It is highly rated, holding a 4.4-star rating from 11 reviews and standing as a local spot. Visitors frequently note a traditional feel and a calm, quiet setting. It remains a worthwhile stop for both locals and visitors to Cairo.

reviews:
Mastabat Al-Mahmal is one of those hidden historical sites in Cairo that many visitors overlook — yet it carries a fascinating cultural and ceremonial legacy. Located near the Citadel area, this structure once played an important role in Egypt’s connection to the annual Hajj pilgrimage.

Historically, the “Mahmal” was a ceremonial palanquin sent from Cairo to Mecca each year, symbolizing the authority and prestige of the ruling power. The Mastabat Al-Mahmal served as the platform or structure associated with this ritual procession. Standing here, you can almost imagine the grand departure ceremonies — decorated camels, musicians, officials, and crowds gathering to witness a deeply meaningful event.

Architecturally, the structure itself is relatively simple compared to Cairo’s ornate mosques and madrasas. However, its understated design gives it a dignified presence. The stonework and elevated platform reflect function over decoration, yet there’s still a sense of historical weight in its proportions.

What I appreciated most about visiting Mastabat Al-Mahmal was its authenticity. It’s not polished or commercialized — it feels like a quiet reminder of Cairo’s role as a spiritual and political center of the Islamic world for centuries. The site invites reflection rather than spectacle.

Because it’s not as crowded as other landmarks, you can take your time absorbing the atmosphere and imagining the ceremonial significance it once held. It adds another layer to understanding Cairo beyond its famous pyramids and grand mosques.

Overall, Mastabat Al-Mahmal is a modest yet meaningful historical site — especially rewarding for travelers interested in Islamic history, pilgrimage traditions, and Cairo’s rich ceremonial past.

The historical significance of the kiosk lies not only in its beauty, but also in its vital role during the reign of Khedive Ismail, as it was used for the grand celebrations marking the dispatch of the Kiswa of the Kaaba to the Holy Lands in the Hijaz. Imagine the grandeur of that scene!

This building, known as the Khedive Ismail Pasha Pavilion, once hosted magnificent farewell ceremonies and processions marking the sending of the Kaaba Cover to Mecca. It's impossible not to feel saddened seeing its current state...

The Reception Hall:

Located above the entrance, this hall was designated for receiving official guests visiting the prince at his palace. It consists of two floors connected by a wooden staircase.

The First Floor: This floor comprises two rooms: The first is the Ceremonial Room, reserved for receiving dignitaries. This hall is distinguished by its stained-glass windows, inlaid with exquisitely crafted stucco. To the right is another small room that served as a sitting room for the women of the harem who accompanied the prince's guests.

The second is the Maghrebi Hall, located opposite the Shami Hall. Designed in the Maghrebi style, it features small Moroccan-style tables and a floor covered with various Turkish carpets.

Upper floor: There is a wonderful and amazing model of the mosque of Sultan Qaytbay al-Mahmudi made of original shells, located on the mastaba that mediates the ladder leading to the upper floor, which consists of two halls. The Gate of Manjaq al-Silahdar is one of the important historical landmarks adorning the "Souq al-Silah" (Arms Market) area in the historic Darb al-Ahmar district of Cairo. It represents part of the remains of a massive palace, of which only this gate remains, testifying to the architectural splendor of the Mamluk era.

Who was Prince Manjaq al-Silahdar?

* Founder: Prince Saif al-Din Manjaq al-Silahdar, one of the senior Mamluk Bahri emirs.

* Position: He held very high positions, including "Silahdar" (responsible for the royal armories) and "Deputy Sultan" during the reign of Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun.

* Date: This gate was built in 1347 CE (748 AH).

Architectural Description of the Gate
Although the palace to which it belonged is no longer in existence, the gate itself is considered an architectural masterpiece:

* Entrance: A high archway built of basalt stone (alternating red and white), a style characteristic of Mamluk architecture. * Decorations: Above the gate is the emblem of Prince Munjaq, the "rank of the Silahdar" (sword), symbolizing his position and confirming his ownership of the site.

* Muqarnas: The top of the entrance is adorned with rows of delicate stone muqarnas, giving the facade an aesthetically pleasing pyramidal shape.

Historical Significance and Location
* Palace Remains: This gate was the main entrance to the palace of Prince Munjaq, which was one of the largest palaces in Cairo during the 14th century.

* The Arms Market: The gate is located on Souq al-Silah Street, a strategic location that connected the Citadel with the old quarters of Cairo. Nearby are important monuments such as the Mosque of al-Jay al-Yusufi and the Bathhouse of Bashtak.

* A Witness to the Era: The gate reflects the power and wealth attained by the Mamluk princes during that period, as their palaces rivaled the grandeur of the sultans' palaces.

Visiting Information
* Location: Souq al-Silah Street, al-Darb al-Ahmar, near the Citadel of Saladin, Cairo. * The experience: Standing before the gate, you can imagine the immense scale of the palace that once stretched beyond, and how the processions of princes passed beneath this majestic stone arch.

The gate is an ideal stop for photography enthusiasts and lovers of Islamic architecture during their tour of the Darb al-Ahmar district.

reviews:
We vacationed in 2018 from February 9, 2018. This was our third time in Egypt. We chose the hotel based on price and location. The reviews were accurate, and we knew where we were going. I won't mention any negatives, as they didn't spoil our vacation. Overall, I'd give the hotel an excellent rating – we were very pleased. The hotel wasn't overcrowded. It was very cozy and quiet.
Check-in was quick, we went up to our room, checked everything in front of a staff member, and picked up our luggage. A little later, a late dinner was delivered. Everything was smooth, calm, and comfortable.
The linens were good, and the towels were excellent. Everything worked in our room. We didn't choose a room; we were assigned the one we were assigned.
We liked the layout of the buildings. Reviews mention the unusual window placement. This is true. Our room had a balcony facing the hallway, and the hallway windows overlooked the courtyard. This location allowed us to rest peacefully. We weren't disturbed by the sounds of the entertainment and nightlife programs on the upper landing near the Mall. I really didn't like the way tea and coffee were served in the restaurant. Despite the excellent pastries (cakes, buns, biscuits, soufflés – all delicious), serving tea and coffee like this really spoiled the experience. I highly recommend management address this.
The hotel has two bars. We mostly used the one at reception. It was very nice to see that the bartender remembered a guest's drink after a couple of days (I also wrote down Fehr Fathy's name). The cocktails were excellent. Not every restaurant has a bartender like that. We used the pool bar during the day; they had ice cream every day and delicious coffee.
I'd also like to commend the hotel staff. They are excellent. They treat tourists well in every way. Starting from reception (we specifically wrote down the names of Ehab and Amr), you can approach them with any question. The language barrier isn't a problem for them. If one employee doesn't understand you, they'll definitely invite someone who will. We had a completely unusual situation, but the guys helped us figure everything out and resolve all the issues.
A huge thank you to everyone, once again.

reviews:
Gate of Qusoun Wakala is a historic architectural landmark in Cairo, representing the commercial and urban design of the Mamluk era. This gate, part of a traditional wakala (caravanserai), showcases impressive stonework, elegant arches, and decorative inscriptions that highlight the craftsmanship of the period.

The structure offers insight into Cairo’s historical trade and social hubs, where merchants lived, stored goods, and conducted business within the same complex. Visitors can appreciate both the functional design and the aesthetic details, making it a fascinating stop for those interested in architecture and history.

Though less visited than major landmarks, the Gate of Qusoun Wakala provides a unique glimpse into Cairo’s commercial and cultural heritage, appealing to history enthusiasts, architecture lovers, and cultural tourists alike.

Only the entryway of this wikala remains. Built in 1330 by Amir Qawsun. His blazon of office, the cup, appears in the roundels of the gateway. It once housed 4000 people. Note the stone slab with hieroglyphics at the base.
A door, and the last piece remaining of a once great trading agency built in the 14th century. … More

The Gate of the Wikala of Qawsun is all that remains today of the once-grand Wikala of Qawsun, a Mamluk commercial caravanserai built in 1341 by the powerful Mamluk amir Qawsun al-Nasiri al-Saqi during the reign of Sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad.

Unfortunately, the main structure was demolished in the 1960s, and only its monumental entrance survived. The gate was preserved, slightly relocated, and raised to match the modern street level. Today it stands as a rare reminder of one of medieval Cairo’s earliest and most important commercial buildings.

Architecturally, the portal is notable for its surviving foundation inscription and the blazon (rank emblem) of Qawsun, who held the office of saqi (cupbearer). The emblem depicts a cup, a common symbol in Mamluk heraldry.

reviews:
The Madrasa and Mosque of Qadi Abu Bakr Mazhar: A Mamluk Gem in Burjwan Alley

Located in the tranquil Burjwan Alley, branching off Al-Muizz Street, the Madrasa and Mosque of Qadi Abu Bakr Mazhar is one of the finest and most exquisite examples of Islamic architecture from the late Circassian Mamluk period. This monument is not merely a mosque, but a complete masterpiece known as the "Pearl of the Qaitbay Era," distinguished by the beauty of its decorations and the precision of its craftsmanship, which continue to amaze visitors.

Founder: A Judge and High-Ranking Administrator

* Builder: This edifice was built by Qadi Zayn al-Din Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Mazhar al-Ansari al-Shafi'i.

* His Status: He was not just a judge, but one of the highest-ranking officials in the state during the reign of Sultan al-Ashraf Qaitbay. He held the highest administrative positions, most notably "Khatib al-Sirr" (Secretary) and "Sahib Diwan al-Insha" (Head of the Chancery), a position equivalent to the head of the Sultan's Diwan, responsible for drafting official state decrees and correspondence. A History of Mamluk Creativity

* Date: The madrasa was built between 1479 and 1480 CE (884-885 AH).

* Significance: This madrasa is considered a prime example of the artistic and architectural sophistication achieved during the golden age of Sultan Qaitbay. Despite its small size compared to other sultanic mosques, it surpasses many in the precision of its details and the beauty of its decorations.

A Complete Architectural Masterpiece
The madrasa dazzles its visitors with its exquisite artistic details in every corner:

* Design: It was designed in the orthogonal plan style of madrasas, with a central courtyard surrounded by four iwans.

* Entrance: It is distinguished by its exceptional beauty, featuring a copper-plated door decorated with intricate geometric patterns (star-shaped medallions).

* Minaret: To the left of the entrance stands a graceful, three-tiered minaret, richly decorated with muqarnas (stalactite-like carvings) in the style of Qaitbay's era. * Interior Decorations (Absolutely Magnificent):

* Minbar: Its minbar is one of the most magnificent Mamluk wooden minbars that have survived in their original state. It is crafted from assembled wood and inlaid with ivory and ebony with exquisite precision.

* Wooden Ceilings: The ceilings of the madrasa are distinguished by their exquisite colorful and gilded decorations.

* Marble Floors: The floor of the courtyard and iwans is a work of art made of multi-colored marble.

* Plaster Windows: The walls of the madrasa are adorned with stucco windows inlaid with stained glass, allowing soft, colored light to filter through, creating an atmosphere of spirituality and beauty.

Visiting Today (August 2025)

* Location: Burjwan Alley, branching off Al-Muizz Street, Al-Gamaliya District.

* Condition: The mosque is in good condition after undergoing restoration work and is open for prayer and visitation.

* Experience: Visiting the Ibn Mazhar Madrasa is a unique experience; it is a hidden gem in a quiet alley, away from the hustle and bustle of the main Al-Muizz Street. It offers visitors a chance to contemplate and appreciate the beauty and precision of Mamluk art at its finest.

The Madrasa of Qadi Abu Bakr Mazhar stands as a testament to the fact that the grandeur of Mamluk architecture was not limited to the sultans, but extended to include prominent statesmen who left an enduring artistic mark in the heart of historic Cairo.
