reviews: A holy place full of peace at the inner Cairo.

St. Catherine's Monastery in Sakakini is one of the hidden historical and spiritual gems in Cairo's Al-Zaher district, administratively affiliated with St. Catherine's Monastery in Sinai.

Key details about this unique place:

1. What is a Metochion?

In the Coptic Orthodox Church, the word "Metochion" means "a branch monastery" or "ecclesiastical representation." This building serves as the official administrative headquarters for St. Catherine's Monastery in Cairo. Historically, it was used as a station for receiving monks and visitors arriving from or traveling to Sinai, and as a storage facility for provisions and documents.

2. Location and Architecture

Location: Situated in the heart of the Sakakini district (Al-Zaher neighborhood), specifically on Sakakini Street near the famous "Sakakini Pasha Palace."

Design: The building features a majestic classical architectural style that reflects the grandeur and antiquity of St. Catherine's Monastery. The monastery includes a small church dedicated to Saint Catherine, characterized by its tranquil and spiritual atmosphere, far removed from the hustle and bustle of the surrounding streets.

Icons: The church houses a collection of magnificent Byzantine icons, similar in style and artistry to those found in the mother monastery in Sinai.

3. Historical and Spiritual Significance
The monastery serves as a link between the heart of Cairo and the holy Sinai.

It is a sacred place for members of the Greek Orthodox community, and visitors come for blessings and prayer, especially those unable to travel to Sinai to visit the original monastery.

The place is distinguished by its profound peace, cleanliness, and order, making it a piece of Sinai in the heart of Cairo.

reviews:
The Khanqah and Madrasa of Tankiz Bugha: A Mamluk Gem in the Heart of Darb al-Ahmar

The madrasa, khanqah, and mausoleum of Prince Saif al-Din Tankiz Bugha, located in the Darb al-Ahmar district of historic Cairo, is one of the finest examples of Mamluk Bahri architecture. It is particularly renowned for its stone dome, considered one of the most beautiful and meticulously crafted domes of that period.

The Founder: Saif al-Din Tankiz Bugha

Prince Saif al-Din Tankiz Bugha was one of the most influential Mamluk princes during the reign of Sultan al-Ashraf Sha'ban ibn Husayn (r. 1363-1377 CE). As was customary for prominent Mamluk princes, Tankiz Bugha was keen to construct an architectural complex to commemorate him and serve as his burial place. He chose a location for it in the heart of vibrant Mamluk Cairo.

A Masterpiece of Mamluk Architecture

Date: This complex was completed in 1362 CE (764 AH).

Function: The complex was multi-purpose, designed as a school for Islamic jurisprudence, a Sufi lodge, a mosque, and a mausoleum dome for the burial of its founder, the prince.

Location: The monument is located on Sidi Madin Street, branching off from Souq al-Silah Street in the Darb al-Ahmar district, an area rich in Mamluk architectural masterpieces.

Key Architectural Elements: The Mausoleum Dome (The Jewel of the Monument):

This is the most famous and beautiful feature of the monument. The stone dome of Tankiz Bugha is considered one of the finest examples of medium-sized Mamluk domes. It is distinguished by its exquisitely carved exterior decorations in the form of zigzag ribs, with remarkable proportions, giving it unparalleled lightness and visual elegance.

The Main Entrance:
This is a soaring stone entrance topped by a three-lobed arch (Madaini) adorned with muqarnas, a typical design for the entrances of grand Mamluk buildings.

The Minaret:

The minaret stands to the left of the entrance. It is a graceful structure built in the Mamluk Bahri style, consisting of a square base topped by an octagonal shaft, and a cylindrical kiosk supporting the minaret's spire.

Current Status and Visiting (July 2025)
Condition: The Khanqah of Tankiz Bugha is a registered monument with the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities. It is generally in good condition and retains many of its original architectural details, especially the dome and the entrance.

Visiting: The site is open to visitors and is a key destination for specialists and enthusiasts of Islamic architecture who wish to explore the hidden treasures of the Darb al-Ahmar district. Although not as famous as the grand mosques of Al-Muizz Street, a visit offers a unique opportunity to appreciate the beauty and precision of Mamluk art up close.

With its elegant dome and intricate details, the Khanqah of Tankiz Bugha stands as a testament to the refined artistic taste achieved by architects and craftsmen during the Mamluk era, and an architectural gem well worth discovering in the heart of historic Cairo.

If you want to spend a unique evening and experience the spirit of Old Cairo, stepping back in time, don't miss a visit to Khan Seddika's house in Darb al-Labbana. Participate in one of their events. The khan is located opposite the Al-Rifai Mosque and the Sultan Hassan Mosque. A steep stone staircase leads up to the alley, and from the first moment you enter, you'll feel a sense of joy and delight in the old doors, staircases, and colorful tiles of the khan. Time flies when you sit on the quiet rooftop overlooking the Citadel of Saladin, which offers a feeling of comfort and tranquility. I was delighted to visit twice and participate in a storytelling evening with a group of people I didn't know, but I felt a sense of camaraderie among them. The second event was a celebration of the khan's first anniversary, featuring religious chanting. The owner of the khan is passionate about historic Cairo and enjoys listening to her stories and tales.

reviews:
Bab al-Barqiyya is a historic city gate in Cairo, reflecting the architectural and defensive ingenuity of the medieval period. The gate features robust stone construction, decorative inscriptions, and elegant arches, showcasing the craftsmanship and design aesthetics of its time.

Visitors can appreciate its strategic and historical significance, as it once served as a key entry point and defensive structure for the city. Its presence offers a tangible connection to Cairo’s past, providing insight into the city’s medieval fortifications and urban planning.

Although less frequented than other major landmarks, Bab al-Barqiyya is a worthwhile stop for history enthusiasts, architecture lovers, and cultural tourists interested in exploring Cairo’s rich Islamic heritage.

The bridge was built about 10 years before the Eiffel Tower and was designed by the same French engineer, Alexandre-Gustave Eiffel.

After more than 20 years of closure, the Eiffel Bridge at the Giza Zoo (west of Cairo), the largest zoo in the Middle East, is once again being discussed.

Earlier this week, Egyptian Minister of Agriculture Sayed El-Quseir announced an agreement between Egypt and France to restore and rehabilitate the Eiffel Bridge at the Zoo, reopening it to the public as a historical facility and part of Egyptian heritage.

The Egyptian Minister toured the area with the French Ambassador to Cairo, Stéphane Romanet, to inspect the condition of the Eiffel Bridge before beginning restoration work. Egypt and France, represented by its embassy in Cairo, agreed to begin restoring the bridge and its entrances, with the aim of creating a new way for visitors to interact with the zoo from the top of the bridge.
This bridge is a testament to Egypt's first suspension tower in Africa.

The Dome of al-Qasid is a surviving Mamluk monument near the historic gate of Bab al-Nasr. It was built in 1334 during the reign of Al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun. … More

🕌 The Dome of al-Qasid – A Forgotten Mamluk Gem in the Heart of al-Gamaliya

The Dome of al-Qasid is a relatively neglected Mamluk Islamic monument, despite its significant historical and architectural value. It is a prime example of the funerary domes that were widespread during the Mamluk era and served as part of the burial system for princes, scholars, and prominent figures in the state.

📍 Location:
Al-Gamaliya Street – Al-Gamaliya District, Cairo.

Near Bab al-Nasr and al-Muizz Street, behind some side alleys branching off from al-Nahhasin Street.

🕰 Construction Date:
Built in the second half of the 8th century AH / 14th century CE.

It dates back to the Bahri Mamluk period or the beginning of the Burji period, but the exact construction date is not 100% certain.

👤 Who was "al-Qasid"?

There are no definitive sources that pinpoint exactly who "al-Qasid" was, but it is generally believed that he was one of the commanders or high-ranking officials of the Mamluk state. 🏛️ Architectural Style:

💠 Layout:
The dome itself is built on a square base that transforms into a circle using muqarnas (stalactite-like decorative elements).

It consists of:

A square base.

A stone dome decorated on the outside.

It likely had a small enclosure or mausoleum attached to it.

🎨 Decoration:
On the outside: The dome is decorated with simple carvings.

It was once partially covered with marble and colored decorations, but most of this has been lost to time and neglect.

It likely contained an inscribed marble tombstone, but its current condition is unclear.

✨ Features:
It represents a rare example of small funerary domes in the heart of Cairo.

It is a clear example of muqarnas art and architectural transformations from a square to a dome.

Despite its simplicity, the dome holds significant heritage value, representing a part of the Mamluk architectural fabric of Al-Gamaliya.

🧭 How to get there:
Nearest metro station: Ataba or Bab El-Sha'riya.

From Al-Muizz Street, walk towards Al-Nahhasin or Wakalat Qaitbay, and ask for "Qubbat Al-Qasid" – it's usually in a side alley, and you'll need someone from the area to guide you.

reviews:
I was looking for Egyptian sculptures and came across this shop that seemed to specialize in them. When I visited, the owner, Ahmed — the same person featured in photos from other reviews — was calmly helping another customer, and it gave me a good first impression. I really thought this place sold genuine, high-quality sculptures, not just the usual tourist souvenirs.

After visiting a few times and asking lots of detailed questions, Ahmed probably saw me as a sure buyer and raised the price accordingly. The price he offered was far above the usual market range, and even the “discounted” price was still pretty high.

I ended up not buying and walked around a bit more. To my surprise, I found several other shops selling almost identical pieces — same material and craftsmanship — for just a fraction of the price after some negotiation. It made me realize that in a big market like this, there’s no reason to rush.

To be fair, this shop does have some beautiful, well-made pieces. But if you visit, check around first and don’t show too much interest right away — you’ll probably get a much better deal elsewhere.

reviews:
The Famine Stele on Sehel Island is a Pharaonic inscription.
At the heart of Sehel Island in Aswan, the stele stands proud, a timeless witness to one of the oldest environmental crises faced by ancient Egypt and to the Egyptians' ingenuity in linking religion with science, and nature with destiny. The Famine Stele is not just a relic… it's a stone cry reminding us that the Nile is the secret of life.

The stele bears a hieroglyphic text consisting of 32 vertical lines, inscribed in the Ptolemaic period, but it tells a story dating back to the reign of King Djoser (Third Dynasty – c. 2686 BC), the most famous king of the Old Kingdom.

Seven lean years, no flood and no harvest. The land is thirsty, and the people are hungry.
King Djoser found no escape except by turning to the wise Imhotep, who explained that the secret of the flood lies in the hands of the god Khnum, the lord of waterfalls and the Nile, ruler of a sacred spring on Elephantine Island.

Divine Vision: After offering sacrifices to the holy trinity (Khnum, Satet, and Anqet), Khnum appeared in the king's dreams, promising that the Nile would return to its normal course and that the famine would end. In fulfillment of this promise, Djoser then ordered the construction of a temple to the god at Elephantine.
